question: Which 1942 film starring Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman is set in French Morocco?
explanation: The script was still being rewritten during filming, and Bergman said she did not know which man her character would leave with until late in the shoot. It won Best Picture, and its most quoted line, 'Play it again, Sam', is never actually said in the film.
hook: Nobody on set knew the ending, and nobody in it says 'Play it again, Sam'.

question: Which band released the album Abbey Road in 1969?
explanation: It was the last album the Beatles recorded together, although Let It Be was released after it in 1970. The zebra-crossing cover was shot in a few minutes outside EMI's studios in St John's Wood, which were later renamed Abbey Road Studios after the album.
hook: The studio was named after the album, not the other way round.

question: Which fictional spy is designated 007?
explanation: Ian Fleming borrowed the name from an American ornithologist whose field guide, Birds of the West Indies, sat on his desk at his Jamaican home, Goldeneye. The 'double-O' prefix means a licence to kill.
hook: The world's most famous spy is named after a birdwatcher.

question: Which Australian soap opera launched the careers of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan?
explanation: Scott and Charlene's wedding drew about twenty million British viewers when it aired there in 1988, more than Australia's whole population at the time. The show ran for forty years before its final episode, number 9,363, in December 2025.
hook: A Ramsay Street wedding outdrew the population of Australia.

question: Which film won eleven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, at the 1998 ceremony?
explanation: Its eleven Oscars from fourteen nominations equalled the record set by Ben-Hur, later matched by The Return of the King. Titanic was also the first film to gross a billion dollars worldwide.
hook: Three films share eleven Oscars: Ben-Hur, Titanic and The Return of the King.

question: Which Australian band recorded the 1980s hit 'Down Under'?
explanation: It topped the charts in Australia, Britain and the United States in 1983. In 2010 a court found its flute riff borrowed from 'Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree', written by Melbourne teacher Marion Sinclair.
hook: The flute line lost a copyright case to a campfire song about a kookaburra.

question: Which television series is set in the fictional Westeros?
explanation: Adapted from George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels, it ran on HBO from 2011 to 2019 and ended before the books did. It won 59 Emmys, a record for a drama series, and the prequel House of the Dragon followed in 2022.
hook: The TV show finished the story before the author did.

question: Which musician was known as the King of Pop?
explanation: Elvis Presley was the King of Rock and Roll and James Brown the Godfather of Soul. Jackson's Thriller (1982) is generally cited as the best-selling album of all time.
hook: Elvis is the King, Jackson the King of Pop, Brown the Godfather of Soul.

question: Which Australian film features Mel Gibson as a police officer in a lawless future?
explanation: Made in 1979 for about $350,000 by George Miller, a Sydney doctor, it took around $100 million worldwide. For twenty years it held the Guinness record for the best return on budget, until The Blair Witch Project in 1999.
hook: Directed by a doctor who had treated real car-crash victims in casualty.

question: Which streaming series features a group of children and a creature called the Demogorgon?
explanation: Set in 1980s Hawkins, Indiana, the Duffer brothers' series borrowed its monster's name from the Dungeons & Dragons game the boys play. It ended on New Year's Eve 2025, with the finale also screened in cinemas.
hook: The kids name the monster after one in their Dungeons & Dragons game.

question: Which band's members included Freddie Mercury and Brian May?
explanation: Brian May built his guitar, the Red Special, with his father, using wood from an old fireplace mantelpiece, and still plays it. He also finished a PhD in astrophysics in 2007, thirty years after he paused it for the band.
hook: The guitarist's guitar came from a fireplace, and he has a doctorate in the stars.

question: Which film franchise features the character Darth Vader?
explanation: Bodybuilder David Prowse wore the suit and James Earl Jones supplied the voice. Prowse was given a dummy line on set, so he only learned 'I am your father' when he watched The Empire Strikes Back.
hook: The man in the suit found out Vader's secret along with the audience.

question: Which Australian actor played Wolverine in the X-Men films?
explanation: He was cast weeks into filming in 2000 after Dougray Scott was held up on Mission: Impossible 2, and played the role on and off until Deadpool & Wolverine in 2024. Eric Bana, the usual wrong answer, played the Hulk in 2003.
hook: A last-minute stand-in who kept the claws for twenty-four years.

question: Which television quiz show made a catchphrase of asking for a final answer?
answer: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?
explanation: It began in Britain in 1998 and has been made in more than a hundred countries. Eddie McGuire hosted the Australian version on Nine, and the lifelines (50:50, phone a friend, ask the audience) became part of everyday speech.
hook: Final answer? Lock it in, Eddie.

question: Which animated film features a clownfish searching for his son?
explanation: The 2003 Pixar film is set on the Great Barrier Reef and in a Sydney dentist's fish tank, with the address 42 Wallaby Way, Sydney. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and the sequel Finding Dory followed in 2016.
hook: P. Sherman, 42 Wallaby Way, Sydney.

question: Which Australian band was fronted by Michael Hutchence?
explanation: Their 1987 album Kick sold millions and produced 'Need You Tonight' and 'Never Tear Us Apart'. After Hutchence died in 1997, the band chose a new singer, J.D. Fortune, through the 2005 reality show Rock Star: INXS.
hook: They found their next frontman through a TV talent show.

question: Which film director made Jaws, E.T. and Jurassic Park?
explanation: The mechanical shark in Jaws broke down so often that Spielberg had to shoot around it, and the unseen threat made the film scarier. He has won Best Director twice, for Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan.
hook: The shark kept breaking, so you barely see it, and that is why it works.

question: Which Australian television drama is set at Summer Bay?
explanation: It began on Seven in 1988, and its beach scenes are filmed at Palm Beach on Sydney's northern beaches. Ray Meagher has played Alf Stewart since the first episode, a Guinness record for the longest-serving actor in an Australian series.
hook: Summer Bay is really Palm Beach, and Alf has been there since day one.

question: Which singer released the album 21 in 2011?
explanation: Named for her age when she wrote it, 21 won six Grammys including Album of the Year and was the world's best-selling album in both 2011 and 2012. Her other albums are 19, 25 and 30.
hook: Her albums are named after her age: 19, 21, 25, 30.

question: Which superhero is also known as the Caped Crusader?
explanation: Created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger in 1939, he has no superpowers, only money, training and gadgets. Superman is the Man of Steel, and Batman's other nickname is the Dark Knight.
hook: Caped Crusader and Dark Knight are Batman; Man of Steel is Superman.

question: Which Australian singer had a global hit with 'Can't Get You Out of My Head' in 2001?
explanation: It reached number one in about forty countries and is her biggest-selling single. She won her first Grammy for 'Come Into My World' in 2004 and a second, for 'Padam Padam', twenty years later.
hook: La la la, la la la-la la: the most famous hum in pop.

question: Which comedy series is set in a New York coffee shop called Central Perk?
explanation: It ran for ten seasons from 1994 to 2004. The six leads bargained as a group, and by the last two seasons each was paid a million US dollars per episode.
hook: Six friends, one couch, a million dollars each per episode.

question: In Casablanca, which song does Rick ask Sam to play?
explanation: Written by Herman Hupfeld in 1931, it was nearly cut because composer Max Steiner wanted his own theme, but Bergman had already cut her hair for another role and the scenes could not be reshot. Rick actually says 'You played it for her, you can play it for me', never 'Play it again, Sam'.
hook: Ingrid Bergman's haircut saved the song.

question: Which Australian investigative journalism program has aired on the ABC since 1961?
explanation: Its 1987 report 'The Moonlight State' exposed Queensland police corruption and led directly to the Fitzgerald Inquiry. The inquiry jailed the state's police commissioner and hastened the end of Joh Bjelke-Petersen's government.
hook: One 1987 episode helped end the Bjelke-Petersen era.

question: Which band recorded 'Bohemian Rhapsody'?
explanation: At almost six minutes with no chorus, the record company thought it far too long for radio. London DJ Kenny Everett played it anyway, and it spent nine weeks at number one in Britain in 1975.
hook: Too long and no chorus, and it was a hit because a DJ ignored the rules.

question: Which streaming service produced the series The Crown?
explanation: Peter Morgan's drama ran from 2016 to 2023 and recast its main roles every two seasons as the royals aged. Claire Foy, Olivia Colman and Imelda Staunton played the Queen, and Australian Elizabeth Debicki played Diana.
hook: Three Queens in six seasons: Foy, Colman, Staunton.

question: Which Australian actor won an Oscar for Gladiator in 2001?
explanation: Crowe, born in New Zealand and raised in Sydney, won Best Actor as the Roman general Maximus. Geoffrey Rush had won Best Actor for Shine four years earlier, and Crowe was nominated again the next year for A Beautiful Mind.
hook: Rush in 1997, Crowe in 2001: two Australian Best Actors in five years.

question: Which 1985 Nintendo game made the plumber Mario and his brother Luigi household names?
explanation: Mario had first appeared in the 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong as a carpenter called Jumpman. Super Mario Bros. sold about forty million copies, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie became one of 2023's biggest films.
hook: He started as a carpenter called Jumpman.

question: Which musical features the song 'Defying Gravity'?
explanation: Based on Gregory Maguire's novel, it retells The Wizard of Oz from the Wicked Witch's side and opened on Broadway in 2003. The film version was split in two: Wicked (2024) and Wicked: For Good (2025), starring Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande.
hook: It is The Wizard of Oz told by the witch, who turns out not to be wicked.

question: Which Australian children's music group formed in Sydney in 1991?
explanation: Anthony Field, Murray Cook and Greg Page met studying early childhood education at Macquarie University and teamed up with Jeff Fatt. They topped BRW's list of Australia's richest entertainers several years running, and Emma Watkins became the first female Wiggle in 2013.
hook: Red, purple, yellow, blue: four shirts, one of the most profitable acts Australia has produced.

question: Which film features a young wizard attending Hogwarts?
answer: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
explanation: The American release was renamed Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, so scenes naming the stone were shot twice. The eight films ran from 2001 to 2011, and HBO is now adapting the books as a series.
hook: Every 'Philosopher's Stone' line was filmed twice, once for America.

question: Which social media platform was founded in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg?
explanation: It began as a network for Harvard students before opening to everyone in 2006. The company bought Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014, and renamed itself Meta in 2021.
hook: It paid a billion dollars for Instagram when Instagram had thirteen staff.

question: For which film did Cate Blanchett win her first Academy Award?
explanation: She won Best Supporting Actress in 2005 for playing Katharine Hepburn in Scorsese's Howard Hughes film, then Best Actress in 2014 for Blue Jasmine. Elizabeth is the common wrong answer: she was nominated for it in 1999 but lost to Gwyneth Paltrow.
hook: She won an Oscar for playing Hepburn, who holds the record for acting Oscars.

question: Which rock band released the album The Dark Side of the Moon?
explanation: Released in 1973, it has spent more than 900 weeks on the US Billboard 200 album chart, far more than any other album. Its songs include 'Money' and 'Time', and it has sold an estimated 45 million copies.
hook: It stayed on the American chart for most of two decades.

question: Which Australian comedy duo created and starred in Kath & Kim?
explanation: Turner played Kath and Riley played her daughter Kim, with Magda Szubanski as Kim's friend Sharon. The show began on the ABC in 2002, sent up the Melbourne suburb of Fountain Lakes, and gave Australians 'look at moiye' and 'noice'.
hook: Noice, different, unusual: Turner is Kath, Riley is Kim.

question: Which film won the first Academy Award for Best Picture in 1929?
distractors: All Quiet on the Western Front
explanation: A silent First World War flying film, Wings was the only silent Best Picture winner until The Artist in 2012. All Quiet on the Western Front won the following year.
hook: The first Best Picture was silent, and the next silent one came 83 years later.

question: Which Beatles album came from the 1967 sessions that also produced 'Strawberry Fields Forever' and 'Penny Lane'?
answer: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
explanation: EMI wanted a single early, so the two songs were released on their own in February 1967 and left off the album, which producer George Martin later called a dreadful mistake. Sgt. Pepper won the Grammy for Album of the Year, the first rock album to do so.
hook: Its two best-known songs from the sessions are not on it.

question: Which Jane Campion film shared the 1993 Palme d'Or at Cannes, making her the first woman to win it?
explanation: Shot in New Zealand with Holly Hunter, it shared the prize with Farewell My Concubine, and Anna Paquin won an Oscar for it aged eleven. Campion went on to win Best Director at the Oscars for The Power of the Dog in 2022.
hook: First woman to win the Palme d'Or, and her child star won an Oscar at eleven.

question: Which television series features the character Walter White?
explanation: Creator Vince Gilligan pitched it as turning Mr Chips into Scarface: a chemistry teacher becomes a drug lord. The spin-off Better Call Saul, about lawyer Saul Goodman, ran for six seasons.
hook: The pitch in one line: Mr Chips becomes Scarface.

question: Which Australian band released the 1987 album Diesel and Dust?
explanation: It was written after the band toured remote Aboriginal communities, and produced 'Beds Are Burning'. Singer Peter Garrett later became federal environment minister and then schools minister in the Rudd and Gillard governments.
hook: The bald singer went from protest songs to the cabinet room.

question: Which film director made Pulp Fiction and Kill Bill?
explanation: Pulp Fiction won the Palme d'Or in 1994 and revived John Travolta's career. Tarantino has long said he will retire after his tenth film, and he won two Oscars for screenwriting, for Pulp Fiction and Django Unchained.
hook: Two screenplay Oscars, and a promise to stop at ten films.

question: Which director made the music video for Michael Jackson's 'Thriller'?
explanation: Jackson hired Landis after seeing his film An American Werewolf in London, and the video runs almost fourteen minutes. Scorsese is a tempting guess because he did direct Jackson's 'Bad' video in 1987.
hook: The werewolf director made the zombie video; Scorsese did 'Bad'.

question: Which Australian film features drag performers crossing the outback in a bus?
answer: The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert
explanation: Released in 1994 and directed by Stephan Elliott, it starred Terence Stamp, Hugo Weaving and Guy Pearce. Lizzy Gardiner and Tim Chappel won the Oscar for costume design, and Gardiner collected it in a dress made of American Express gold cards.
hook: An Oscar for costumes, collected in a dress made of credit cards.

question: Which animated sitcom is set in the fictional town of Springfield?
explanation: Matt Groening picked the name because it is one of the most common town names in America, and the show deliberately never reveals its state. Family Guy is set in Quahog, Rhode Island, and King of the Hill in Arlen, Texas.
hook: Springfield could be anywhere, and the show makes sure it stays that way.

question: Which musician wrote and performed 'Purple Rain'?
explanation: The song and its 1984 film won Prince an Oscar for Best Original Song Score. He played most instruments on his records himself, and in 1993 he changed his name to an unpronounceable symbol during a fight with Warner Bros.
hook: He became a symbol to escape his record contract.

question: Which Australian film comedy features the Kerrigan family fighting to keep their home?
explanation: Made by the Working Dog team in about eleven days in 1997, it follows Darryl Kerrigan's fight against the compulsory acquisition of his house next to the airport. 'It's the vibe', 'Tell him he's dreamin'' and 'How's the serenity?' all entered Australian speech.
hook: It's the vibe of the thing: eleven days' filming, a lifetime of quotes.

question: Which film featuring Hannibal Lecter won the five major Oscars in 1992?
explanation: It is one of only three films to win Picture, Director, Actor, Actress and Screenplay, after It Happened One Night and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. Anthony Hopkins won Best Actor with about sixteen minutes on screen.
hook: Best Actor for about sixteen minutes of screen time.

question: In which year did the ABC children's program Play School first air?
explanation: It began in July 1966, adapted from a BBC format, and is often described as the second-longest-running children's show in the world. Its toys, including Big Ted, Little Ted, Jemima and Humpty, outlast every presenter.
hook: On air since 1966, looking through the round, square and arched windows.

question: Which band's 1991 album Nevermind popularised grunge?
explanation: In January 1992 it knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous off the top of the US album chart, the moment alternative rock went mainstream. The cover baby swimming towards a dollar note was Spencer Elden, then four months old.
hook: The Seattle band knocked the King of Pop off number one.

question: Which film series features the character Ellen Ripley?
explanation: Dan O'Bannon's script left the crew's genders open, and casting Sigourney Weaver made Ripley one of cinema's first female action leads. She was nominated for an Oscar for the 1986 sequel Aliens, rare for a science-fiction role.
hook: The script never said Ripley was a man or a woman.

question: Which Australian musician released the album Murder Ballads in 1996?
explanation: Recorded with the Bad Seeds, it included his biggest chart hit, 'Where the Wild Roses Grow', a duet with Kylie Minogue in which his character kills hers. It reached number two in Australia.
hook: His biggest hit is a duet in which he murders Kylie.

question: Which film won Best Picture at the Academy Awards ceremony held in March 1994?
explanation: Spielberg shot it in black and white and refused a salary, calling any fee 'blood money'. Forrest Gump, the usual wrong answer, is a 1994 film and won at the following year's ceremony.
hook: Ceremony year and film year differ: Schindler at the 1994 show, Gump at 1995.

question: Which Australian actor starred in Brokeback Mountain and The Dark Knight?
explanation: He won Best Supporting Actor for playing the Joker in 2009, a year after his death, only the second posthumous acting Oscar. The first also went to someone raised in Australia: Peter Finch, for Network in 1977.
hook: Both posthumous acting Oscars went to men who grew up in Australia.

question: Which television series is set in Baltimore's drug trade and police department?
explanation: Created by former Baltimore Sun police reporter David Simon, it ran on HBO from 2002 to 2008. It never won an Emmy, yet regularly tops critics' lists of the greatest television series.
hook: No Emmys, and top of almost every all-time list.

question: Which singer was known as the Queen of Soul?
explanation: Her 1967 'Respect' was originally an Otis Redding song, and she added the famous R-E-S-P-E-C-T spelling. In 1987 she became the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
hook: Otis wrote it, Aretha spelled it out.

question: Which Australian film about a radio telescope and the Apollo 11 broadcast was released in 2000?
explanation: Made by the same Working Dog team as The Castle, it is set at Parkes Observatory in New South Wales, which relayed most of the moonwalk TV pictures to about 600 million people. The first few minutes actually came through Honeysuckle Creek near Canberra, which the film leaves out.
hook: The moonwalk reached the world via a dish in a Parkes sheep paddock.

question: Which band released 'Stairway to Heaven'?
explanation: It appeared on their untitled fourth album in 1971 and was never released as a single in Britain or America. A US jury decided in 2016 that its opening did not copy Spirit's 'Taurus', and an appeals court upheld that in 2020.
hook: Rock radio's most famous song was never a single.

question: Which film director made Vertigo, Psycho and North by Northwest?
explanation: He was nominated five times for Best Director and never won. His Rebecca did win Best Picture in 1941, but that Oscar went to producer David O. Selznick.
hook: The Master of Suspense never won a directing Oscar.

question: Which Australian comedy team drove a fake Canadian motorcade into the APEC security zone in Sydney in 2007?
explanation: Chas Licciardello, dressed as Osama bin Laden, stepped out near the leaders' hotel before police noticed. The stunt was filmed for The Chaser's War on Everything on the ABC, and charges against the team were later dropped.
hook: 'Bin Laden' got out of the car before anyone checked the passes.

question: Which singer recorded 'My Heart Will Go On' for the film Titanic?
explanation: James Cameron did not want a pop song, so composer James Horner had Dion record a demo in secret, and that single take is the version released. It won the Oscar for Best Original Song and topped charts around the world in 1998.
hook: The director did not want it, and the secret demo is what you hear.

question: For which film did Nicole Kidman win the Academy Award for Best Actress?
explanation: She won in 2003 for playing Virginia Woolf, with a prosthetic nose. Kidman and Cate Blanchett (Blue Jasmine) are the only Australians to have won Best Actress.
hook: She won it with a fake nose, playing a real writer.

question: Which video game franchise features the character Lara Croft?
explanation: Created by British studio Core Design in 1996, it was one of the first blockbuster games with a female lead. Angelina Jolie played her on film in 2001 and Alicia Vikander in 2018.
hook: A 1996 archaeologist who later became Angelina Jolie.

question: Which Australian film features Toni Collette and ABBA songs at a wedding?
explanation: Set in the fictional Queensland town of Porpoise Spit, P.J. Hogan's 1994 film came out the same year as Priscilla, which also leans on ABBA. Collette put on weight for the role, and Rachel Griffiths played Muriel's friend Rhonda.
hook: 'You're terrible, Muriel': Porpoise Spit and a lot of ABBA.

question: Which drummer did Ringo Starr replace in the Beatles in 1962?
explanation: Best was sacked in August 1962, weeks before the first single 'Love Me Do'. Stuart Sutcliffe, the usual wrong answer, was their early bass player, and Jimmy Nicol filled in for Ringo on tour in 1964.
hook: Best was not the best fit: out weeks before the first record.

question: Which ABC series starring Richard Roxburgh follows the chaotic Sydney barrister Cleaver Greene?
explanation: It ran from 2010 to 2018 and was loosely inspired by Sydney barrister Charles Waterstreet. An American remake with Greg Kinnear lasted one season in 2014.
hook: A barrister who is always in trouble, based on a real one.

question: Which film features the line 'I'm going to make him an offer he can't refuse'?
distractors: Once Upon a Time in America
explanation: Marlon Brando stuffed tissues in his cheeks for his screen test to give Vito Corleone his jowls, and the studio had not wanted him. He won Best Actor and refused the Oscar, sending Sacheen Littlefeather to decline it.
hook: Brando won the part with tissues in his cheeks and then refused the Oscar.

question: Which 2020 streaming series follows an orphaned chess prodigy named Beth Harmon?
explanation: Based on Walter Tevis's 1983 novel and starring Anya Taylor-Joy, it led to a surge in chess-set sales and online chess sign-ups. The Queen's Gambit is a real chess opening: 1.d4 d5 2.c4.
hook: Named after a real opening, and it sold out chess sets worldwide.

question: Which Australian rock band recorded 'Khe Sanh'?
explanation: Written by Don Walker about a Vietnam veteran who cannot settle back home, it was released in 1978 and restricted on commercial radio for its lyrics. It only reached number 41, yet it is one of the best-known Australian songs.
hook: Barely a hit, and every Australian pub knows the words.

question: Which animation studio produced Toy Story?
explanation: Toy Story (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature. Steve Jobs bought Pixar's forerunner from George Lucas in 1986 for about ten million dollars and sold it to Disney in 2006 for about 7.4 billion.
hook: Ten million from George Lucas, 7.4 billion from Disney.

question: Which band released the 1977 album Rumours, written while its two couples were breaking up?
explanation: Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks were splitting up, as were John and Christine McVie, and Mick Fleetwood was divorcing too. Songs like 'Go Your Own Way' and 'Dreams' are the band members writing about each other.
hook: 'Go Your Own Way' and 'Dreams' are exes answering each other.

question: Which Australian drama series dramatised Melbourne's gangland war from 2008?
explanation: A court banned the first season from being shown in Victoria, where the killings happened, to protect a murder trial, so many Victorians watched pirated copies instead. Later seasons covered Sydney's Kings Cross and 1970s drug trade.
hook: Banned in the very state it was about.

question: Which film features a shark terrorising the town of Amity Island?
explanation: Released in 1975 and filmed on Martha's Vineyard, it is credited with creating the summer blockbuster through a wide release and TV advertising. The crew nicknamed the mechanical shark Bruce, after Spielberg's lawyer.
hook: The shark was called Bruce, after a lawyer.

question: Which Australian singer-songwriter recorded 'To Her Door' and 'How to Make Gravy'?
explanation: 'How to Make Gravy' is a letter from a prisoner written on 21 December, so fans mark that date as Gravy Day. Kelly also co-wrote 'From Little Things Big Things Grow' with Kev Carmody.
hook: 21 December is Gravy Day, because of one Paul Kelly song.

question: Which sitcom featured the characters Jerry, George, Elaine and Kramer?
explanation: Created by Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, it was called 'a show about nothing', and the writers' rule was 'no hugging, no learning'. George Costanza was based largely on Larry David himself.
hook: No hugging, no learning.

question: Which film franchise features the Millennium Falcon?
explanation: The original design looked too much like the Eagle from the British series Space: 1999, so it was redesigned into the familiar flying saucer shape. The first design was kept and became Princess Leia's ship, the Tantive IV.
hook: Han Solo's ship was redesigned to avoid copying a British TV show.

question: How many Academy Awards did The Color Purple win from eleven nominations?
explanation: Spielberg's 1985 film shares the record for most nominations without a win with The Turning Point (1977), which also went eleven for none. A musical remake of The Color Purple was released in 2023.
hook: Eleven nominations, zero statues, and it has happened twice.

question: Which director made the 1994 Australian comedy Muriel's Wedding?
explanation: Hogan next made My Best Friend's Wedding (1997) in Hollywood. Stephan Elliott directed Priscilla the same year, Baz Luhrmann Strictly Ballroom in 1992 and Rob Sitch The Castle in 1997.
hook: Hogan made two 'Wedding' films: Muriel's, then My Best Friend's.

question: Which song's bassline did Vanilla Ice use without permission in 'Ice Ice Baby'?
explanation: The riff comes from Queen and David Bowie's 1981 duet. Vanilla Ice claimed his version was different because of one extra note, then settled and gave them songwriting credits. 'Super Freak' is the sample in MC Hammer's 'U Can't Touch This'.
hook: His defence was one extra note. It did not work.

question: In which year did television broadcasting begin in Australia?
explanation: TCN-9 in Sydney went to air on 16 September 1956 with Bruce Gyngell saying 'Good evening, and welcome to television'. Melbourne stations launched in time for the Olympics that November.
hook: Australia got TV just in time for the Melbourne Olympics.

question: Which 2020 animated film's release straight to home rental sparked a fight between Universal and the AMC cinema chain?
explanation: With cinemas shut by the pandemic, Universal released it for home rental in April 2020 and then suggested it would keep doing so. AMC threatened to stop showing all Universal films, and the two later agreed a shorter cinema window.
hook: A kids' cartoon started the war between studios and cinemas.

question: Which Sydney band had a 1966 international hit with 'Friday on My Mind'?
explanation: It was written by band members Harry Vanda and George Young, who later produced AC/DC's early albums. George's younger brothers Malcolm and Angus Young founded AC/DC.
hook: The Easybeats' George Young was AC/DC's big brother.

question: Which film director has won the most Academy Awards for Best Director?
explanation: Ford won four, for The Informer, The Grapes of Wrath, How Green Was My Valley and The Quiet Man, and none was for a western. Wyler and Capra won three each.
hook: The king of westerns won four directing Oscars and none for a western.

question: Which Australian-raised group wrote much of the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack?
explanation: The Gibb brothers were born on the Isle of Man and grew up in Redcliffe, Queensland, where they started performing. In March 1978 they wrote five of the songs in the US top ten at the same time.
hook: Redcliffe boys who once had five songs in the US top ten at once.

question: Which television series holds the record for the most Primetime Emmy Awards?
explanation: Counting its Creative Arts awards, SNL has passed 110 Emmys since 1975, nearly twice Game of Thrones' 59, the record for a drama. Lorne Michaels has produced it for almost all of its fifty years.
hook: Fifty years on air beats any single great drama.

question: Which Australian film was nominated for the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar in 2017?
explanation: Shot on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu with local villagers as the cast, it tells a true story of forbidden love. It is the only Australian film nominated in that category, and it did not win.
hook: Australia's only nomination in the category was filmed in Vanuatu.

question: Which song held the US Billboard Hot 100 record of 22 weeks at number one until Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' passed it in September 2026?
answer: All I Want for Christmas Is You by Mariah Carey
distractors: Old Town Road by Lil Nas X
One Sweet Day by Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men
explanation: Mariah Carey's 1994 song did not reach number one until December 2019, then returned every Christmas to build up 22 weeks. 'Choosin' Texas' took the record with its 23rd week on the chart dated 26 September 2026.
hook: Twenty-five years to reach number one, then a record built one December at a time.

question: Which Australian played James Bond in On Her Majesty's Secret Service?
explanation: A former car salesman from Goulburn working as a model in London, he had never acted when cast in 1969. On advice from his manager, he walked away from a seven-film deal after one film.
hook: One film, no acting experience, and he turned down six more.

question: Which record label rejected the Beatles in 1962, reportedly saying guitar groups were on the way out?
explanation: Decca's Dick Rowe signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead, a London band. George Martin then signed the Beatles to Parlophone, part of EMI.
hook: Decca declined; Parlophone signed them.

question: Which was the first sequel to win the Academy Award for Best Picture?
distractors: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
explanation: It won in 1975, and The Return of the King (2004) is the only other sequel to win. Marlon Brando and Robert De Niro both won Oscars for playing Vito Corleone, and the Joker later did the same for Heath Ledger and Joaquin Phoenix.
hook: Two sequels have won Best Picture: Godfather II and Return of the King.

question: Which Australian television music program ran on the ABC from 1974 to 1987?
explanation: Ian 'Molly' Meldrum's Sunday-night interviews and tips could make a record a hit, and it helped ABBA break through worldwide. Rage replaced it in 1987 and still runs overnight on weekends.
hook: Do yourself a favour: Molly's word made hits.

question: Which actor has received the most Academy Award acting nominations?
explanation: Streep has 21 nominations and three wins. Katharine Hepburn holds the record for wins with four, and Jack Nicholson has the most nominations for a man, with twelve.
hook: Streep for nominations, Hepburn for wins.

question: Which Australian film director made Moulin Rouge! and The Great Gatsby?
explanation: Strictly Ballroom, Romeo + Juliet and Moulin Rouge! form his 'Red Curtain' trilogy, designed with his wife Catherine Martin, who has won four Oscars. His 2022 film Elvis was shot on the Gold Coast.
hook: Three films behind the Red Curtain, and his wife has four Oscars.

question: Which Pink Floyd album cover shows a prism splitting light into a spectrum?
answer: The Dark Side of the Moon
explanation: Designed by Storm Thorgerson and Aubrey Powell's studio Hipgnosis, the cover has no band name or title. Animals is the one with the inflatable pig over Battersea Power Station.
hook: A prism for Dark Side, a pig for Animals.

question: Which television series was cancelled after one season in 2002 and later became a cult film?
explanation: Fox aired Joss Whedon's space western out of order and showed only eleven of its fourteen episodes. Strong DVD sales paid for the 2005 film Serenity.
hook: Aired in the wrong order, then blamed for its ratings.

question: How many Academy Awards did Mad Max: Fury Road win in 2016?
explanation: All six were craft awards, including editing, costume and production design, the most Oscars for an Australian film. Editor Margaret Sixel, George Miller's wife, had never cut an action film before.
hook: Six Oscars, and one went to the director's wife.

question: Which musician won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature and did not publicly acknowledge it for about two weeks?
explanation: He skipped the Stockholm ceremony, and Patti Smith sang his 'A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall' in his place, stopping when she forgot the words. He delivered the required Nobel lecture months later.
hook: Patti Smith sang his song and lost her place, and he did not turn up.

question: Which video game has sold more than 350 million copies, the most of any single game?
explanation: Released in 2011 by Swedish studio Mojang, which Microsoft bought for 2.5 billion US dollars in 2014, it reached 350 million sales in 2025. A Minecraft Movie took nearly a billion dollars that year. Tetris is sometimes given as the answer, but only by counting all its versions together.
hook: Tetris wins only if you add up every version; Minecraft wins as one game.

question: Which Australian actress starred in Muriel's Wedding and The Sixth Sense?
explanation: She put on about 18 kilograms to play Muriel and was nominated for an Oscar for The Sixth Sense five years later. Rachel Griffiths, the usual wrong answer, played Muriel's best friend Rhonda.
hook: Collette was Muriel; Griffiths was Rhonda.

question: Which film was the first to gross a billion dollars worldwide?
distractors: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
explanation: It passed the mark in 1998. James Cameron also made Avatar (2009), still the highest-grossing film, and its sequels The Way of Water and Fire and Ash, so he has directed four billion-dollar films.
hook: First to a billion was Cameron, and he has done it three times since with the Avatar films.

question: Which band famously performed on a London rooftop in January 1969?
explanation: Their last public performance was on the roof of Apple Corps at 3 Savile Row, and police stopped it after about forty-two minutes. John Lennon closed with 'I hope we've passed the audition'.
hook: Their last gig ended with a joke about passing the audition.

question: Which 2016 ABC series set Aboriginal Dreaming figures in a science-fiction Sydney?
explanation: Created by Ryan Griffen, it cast the Hairypeople of Aboriginal oral tradition as a persecuted minority in a near-future city. It was co-produced with America's SundanceTV and screened overseas.
hook: Dreaming stories told as science fiction.

question: Which composer wrote the scores for Star Wars, Jaws and Indiana Jones?
explanation: With more than fifty nominations he is the most-nominated living person in Oscar history, second only to Walt Disney. Spielberg laughed when Williams first played him the two-note Jaws theme, thinking it was a joke.
hook: Spielberg thought the Jaws theme was a joke.

question: Which television network first broadcast The Simpsons as shorts before its own series?
answer: Fox, on The Tracey Ullman Show
distractors: CBS, on The Carol Burnett Show
explanation: Matt Groening sketched the family in producer James L. Brooks's lobby, naming them after his own family, and the shorts began in 1987. The half-hour series started in December 1989.
hook: Homer, Marge, Lisa and Maggie are named after Groening's own family.

question: Which barrister was the first host of the ABC's Media Watch in 1989?
explanation: He hosted until 1997 and set its sarcastic tone. Later hosts include Richard Ackland, David Marr, Monica Attard, Jonathan Holmes and Paul Barry, and Linton Besser took over in 2025.
hook: A barrister started it, which explains the cross-examination style.

question: Which film's opening weekend record was broken by Avengers: Endgame in 2019?
explanation: Endgame took about 357 million US dollars in North America in its first three days, well ahead of Infinity War's 258 million a year earlier. It went on to become the second-highest-grossing film ever, behind Avatar.
hook: It broke its own predecessor's record, set one year before.

question: Which Australian band's 1980 album Back in Black is among the best-selling records of all time?
explanation: Recorded months after singer Bon Scott died, with Brian Johnson replacing him, its all-black cover was a sign of mourning. Estimates put its sales at about 50 million, second only to Thriller.
hook: The black cover is a mourning band for Bon Scott.

question: Which director's 1971 television film Duel pitted a motorist against an unseen truck driver?
explanation: The truck driver is never properly shown, the same restraint Spielberg used with the shark in Jaws four years later. His first cinema feature was The Sugarland Express in 1974.
hook: You never see the driver, and you barely see the shark.

question: Which musician holds the record for the most Grammy Awards won?
explanation: She passed conductor Georg Solti's 31 in 2023 and reached 35 in 2025, when Cowboy Carter finally won her Album of the Year. The 2026 Album of the Year went to Bad Bunny, the first Spanish-language winner.
hook: The record had belonged to a classical conductor for twenty-six years.

question: Which 2002 Australian film follows three Aboriginal girls walking home after being taken to a settlement?
explanation: Directed by Phillip Noyce, it is based on Doris Pilkington Garimara's book about her mother Molly's escape from the Moore River settlement in 1931. The girls walked for about nine weeks, following the fence home to Jigalong.
hook: They found their way home by following a rabbit fence.

question: Which television series finale was watched by around 105 million American viewers in 1983?
explanation: 'Goodbye, Farewell and Amen' is still the most-watched scripted episode in US history. The series ran for eleven years, nearly four times as long as the Korean War it was set in.
hook: The show lasted almost four times longer than its war.

question: Which film introduced the character Indiana Jones?
distractors: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom
Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
explanation: In the 1981 film, a long whip-versus-sword fight was replaced by Indy simply shooting the swordsman, because Harrison Ford had dysentery. Temple of Doom (1984) is actually a prequel, set a year earlier.
hook: The film's best gag happened because the star was too sick to fight.

question: Which singer's posthumous album Djarimirri was the first in an Indigenous language to top the ARIA albums chart?
explanation: Blind from birth, the Yolŋu singer from Elcho Island sang mostly in his own languages and rarely gave interviews. Djarimirri reached number one in 2018, the year after his death.
hook: A number-one album with almost no English on it.

question: Which film was the first animated feature to be nominated for Best Picture?
distractors: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
explanation: Disney's 1991 film was nominated at the 1992 Oscars. A separate Best Animated Feature award began in 2002 (won by Shrek), and since then Up and Toy Story 3 have also been Best Picture nominees.
hook: Belle got animation into the top category first.

question: Which band recorded the album OK Computer in 1997?
explanation: Much of it was recorded at St Catherine's Court, an old manor house near Bath then owned by actress Jane Seymour. Its songs about technology and alienation, including 'Paranoid Android', are often called prophetic about the internet age.
hook: A Bond girl's country house produced the album about computer-age dread.

question: Which Australian actor played the lead in the 1979 film My Brilliant Career?
explanation: Gillian Armstrong directed it, the first Australian feature directed by a woman in almost fifty years. Davis played Sybylla, from Miles Franklin's 1901 novel, and Franklin's name is now on Australia's top literary prize.
hook: Miles Franklin's novel, the prize now named after her.

question: Which South Korean writer-director created the Netflix series Squid Game?
explanation: He wrote it around 2009 but it was rejected for ten years as too grim. Its 2021 first season became Netflix's most-watched series, and the show ended with its third season in 2025.
hook: Rejected for a decade, then Netflix's biggest series.

question: Which Australian comedy film starring Paul Hogan was the highest-grossing film of 1986 in Australia?
explanation: It is still the highest-grossing Australian film at the Australian box office, and in the United States it was second for 1986, behind only Top Gun. 'That's not a knife' is its best-known line.
hook: That's not a knife: second only to Top Gun in America.

question: Which single is the best-selling physical single of all time?
explanation: Bing Crosby's 1942 recording of Irving Berlin's song has estimated sales above fifty million. Elton John's 1997 tribute to Princess Diana is the best-selling single since reliable charts began.
hook: A wartime Christmas song still outsells everything since.

question: Which Oppenheimer actor won Best Supporting Actor at the 2024 Oscars for playing Lewis Strauss?
explanation: Oppenheimer won seven Oscars, including Best Picture and Best Director, Christopher Nolan's first. Cillian Murphy won Best Actor in the title role, while Ryan Gosling was nominated for playing Ken in Barbie.
hook: Iron Man won his first Oscar playing Oppenheimer's enemy.

question: Which prison drama, first shown in 1997, was HBO's first hour-long drama series?
explanation: Tom Fontana's series ran for six seasons and showed HBO could make violent adult drama that network TV could not. The Sopranos followed in 1999 and is usually credited with starting the prestige TV era.
hook: Before Tony Soprano, there was a prison called Oz.

question: Which Australian director made Happy Feet and Babe: Pig in the City as well as the Mad Max films?
explanation: Miller, a trained doctor, won his only Oscar for Happy Feet, the 2006 dancing-penguin film. He co-wrote and produced the first Babe, but Chris Noonan directed it.
hook: The Mad Max director's Oscar is for dancing penguins.

question: Which Beach Boys album did Paul McCartney name as the biggest influence on Sgt. Pepper?
explanation: Brian Wilson made Pet Sounds (1966) partly in response to the Beatles' Rubber Soul, and McCartney answered it with Sgt. Pepper. McCartney called 'God Only Knows' one of the best songs ever written.
hook: Rubber Soul led to Pet Sounds, which led to Sgt. Pepper.

question: Which Australian television personality hosted the variety show Hey Hey It's Saturday?
explanation: It ran on Nine from 1971 to 1999, starting as a Saturday morning cartoon show before moving to prime time. Somers's sidekick was Ossie Ostrich, operated by Ernie Carroll.
hook: Daryl and a puppet ostrich, for nearly thirty years.

question: Which film features a character repeating the same day over and over in Punxsutawney?
explanation: Bill Murray plays a weatherman stuck on 2 February. Director Harold Ramis first estimated the loop lasted about ten years and later said thirty or forty, and the title is now an everyday phrase for repetition.
hook: The title became an everyday phrase for the same thing happening again.

question: Who co-wrote the 1985 charity single 'We Are the World' with Michael Jackson?
explanation: Quincy Jones produced it, with a sign on the studio door reading 'Please check your ego at the door'. It raised more than 60 million US dollars for famine relief in Africa, following Britain's Band Aid.
hook: Richie and Jackson wrote it, Jones made the stars check their egos.

question: Which Seven Network drama about a Sydney hospital ward ran from 1998 to 2009?
explanation: It began on Ward 17 of the fictional All Saints Western General Hospital and later moved to the emergency department. GP and MDA were ABC medical dramas, and The Flying Doctors was set in outback New South Wales.
hook: Twelve years at All Saints, Ward 17.

question: Which film won Best Picture at the 2020 Academy Awards, the first non-English language film to do so?
explanation: Bong Joon-ho's film also won Director, Original Screenplay and International Feature, the first film to win both Best Picture and the international award. It had already won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2019.
hook: Cannes and the Oscars' top prize with the same film.

question: In which Western Australian city is AC/DC singer Bon Scott buried?
explanation: Born in Scotland, Scott grew up in Fremantle, and his grave there was added to the state heritage register in 2006. A bronze statue of him stands at the Fremantle Fishing Boat Harbour.
hook: The singer's grave is heritage-listed.

question: Which television format originated in the Netherlands in 1999 and spread worldwide?
explanation: Created by John de Mol's Endemol and named after the watcher in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, it made the surveillance house a staple of 2000s television. De Mol later created The Voice, and Survivor began in Sweden in 1997.
hook: Named after Orwell's all-seeing dictator.

question: Which Australian film won the Camera d'Or at Cannes in 2009 for Warwick Thornton?
explanation: The Camera d'Or is the prize for best first feature, and Thornton shot it around Alice Springs with two untrained teenage leads and very little dialogue. He later directed Sweet Country (2017).
hook: Two untrained teenagers, almost no dialogue, and a Cannes prize.

question: Which Brisbane-made animated series follows a Blue Heeler puppy and her family?
explanation: Created by Joe Brumm and made by Ludo Studio, it first aired on ABC Kids in 2018 and reached the world through Disney+. It has become one of the most-streamed shows in the United States, and The Sign was its longest episode.
hook: Bluey is a Blue Heeler; her sister Bingo is a Red Heeler.

question: Who directed the 2023 film Barbie, starring Margot Robbie?
explanation: It was the highest-grossing film of 2023 and made Gerwig the first woman to direct a billion-dollar film on her own. It opened the same day as Oppenheimer, and the double bill was nicknamed Barbenheimer.
hook: Barbenheimer: Gerwig's pink film opened against Nolan's bomb.

question: Which singer's Eras Tour became the first concert tour to gross more than US$2 billion?
explanation: It ran for 149 shows from March 2023 to December 2024, including three at the MCG and four in Sydney in February 2024. The previous record, Elton John's farewell tour, took under a billion.
hook: She roughly doubled the old touring record.

question: Which 2025 animated film became Netflix's most-watched film ever, helped by the hit song 'Golden'?
explanation: Made by Sony Pictures Animation for Netflix, it follows a girl group secretly fighting demons. 'Golden' spent weeks at number one in the US, won the Golden Globe for Best Original Song and won a Grammy in 2026.
hook: A fictional girl group had a real number-one hit.

question: Which singer broke through in 2021 with the break-up ballad 'drivers license'?
explanation: Rodrigo was then an actor in Disney's High School Musical: The Musical: The Series, and the song debuted at number one in the US and Australia. Fans guessed the 'blonde girl' in the lyrics was Sabrina Carpenter, another Disney actor.
hook: A Disney actor who had just got her driver's licence.

question: Which film won Best Picture at the Academy Awards in March 2026?
explanation: Paul Thomas Anderson's comedy-thriller starring Leonardo DiCaprio won six Oscars, including Anderson's first for directing. Sinners had set a record with sixteen nominations, and its star Michael B. Jordan won Best Actor.
hook: Anderson's first Oscar came with his Best Picture.

question: Which K-pop group's members are RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V and Jungkook?
explanation: In 2020 'Dynamite' made them the first all-South Korean act to top the US Hot 100. All seven completed compulsory military service by June 2025, which had paused the group.
hook: Seven members, one national service break.

question: Which actor played the title role in Baz Luhrmann's 2022 film Elvis?
explanation: Shot on the Gold Coast with Tom Hanks as Colonel Tom Parker, it earned Butler an Oscar nomination. A year later Australian Jacob Elordi played Elvis in Sofia Coppola's Priscilla, which is why his name is the usual wrong answer.
hook: Butler was Luhrmann's Elvis; Elordi was Coppola's.

question: Which 2023 single won Kylie Minogue the first Grammy ever given for Best Pop Dance Recording?
explanation: It was her second Grammy, twenty years after 'Come Into My World', and came from her album Tension. The title imitates the sound of a heartbeat.
hook: Padam padam is a heartbeat, and it beat twenty years after her first Grammy.

question: Which singer represented Australia at Eurovision 2026 in Vienna, finishing fourth with 'Eclipse'?
explanation: It was Australia's best result since Dami Im came second in 2016. Bulgaria won for the first time, with DARA's 'Bangaranga'.
hook: Fourth place: Australia's best Eurovision since Dami Im.

question: Which country won its first Eurovision Song Contest in 2026 with DARA's 'Bangaranga'?
explanation: The final was held in Vienna after Austria's JJ won in 2025 with 'Wasted Love'. Bulgaria won both the jury and public votes, by a margin of 173 points, the biggest in the contest's history.
hook: Bangaranga brought Bulgaria its first win by a record margin.

question: Which actor, who played Irene Roberts on Home and Away for more than thirty years, won the 2025 Gold Logie?
explanation: McGranger had played Irene, owner of the Summer Bay Diner, since 1993, making her one of the show's longest-serving cast members after Ray Meagher. The 2026 Gold Logie went to comedian Sam Pang.
hook: Irene Roberts, over thirty years at the Diner, finally took the Gold.

question: Which song topped triple j's first Hottest 100 of Australian Songs in July 2025?
explanation: The countdown marked triple j's fiftieth anniversary and was the first Hottest 100 limited to Australian songs from any year. INXS released it on their 1987 album Kick, and it was played as Michael Hutchence's coffin was carried out at his 1997 funeral.
hook: triple j turned fifty and INXS won.

question: Which song won triple j's Hottest 100 of 2025, counted down in January 2026?
distractors: 'Paint the Town Red' by Doja Cat
explanation: The English singer made it three female solo winners in a row, after Doja Cat for 2023 and Chappell Roan for 2024. The other options are the previous winners and a 2024 hit.
hook: Doja, Chappell, then Dean: three women in a row.

question: Which Australian actress earned a 2026 Best Actress Oscar nomination for If I Had Legs I'd Kick You?
explanation: It was the Sydney-born actress's first Oscar nomination, and Jessie Buckley won the award for Hamnet. Byrne is also known for Bridesmaids and the comedy Neighbors.
hook: Her film Neighbors was renamed Bad Neighbours in Australia, to avoid confusion with the soap.

question: Which FX series set a record of 18 Emmy wins for a single season in 2024?
explanation: Based on James Clavell's novel and mostly in Japanese, it beat John Adams's record of 13. Anna Sawai and Hiroyuki Sanada became the first Japanese actors to win lead acting Emmys.
hook: A drama mostly in Japanese won more Emmys in one year than any series before.

question: Which film won Best Picture at the 2025 Academy Awards?
explanation: Sean Baker won four Oscars that night, for Picture, Director, Original Screenplay and Editing, equalling Walt Disney's 1954 record for one person at one ceremony. Mikey Madison won Best Actress for the title role.
hook: One man took four statues home for one film.

question: Which series follows a fine-dining chef who returns to run his family's Chicago sandwich shop?
explanation: Jeremy Allen White plays Carmy Berzatto, and the shop is The Original Beef of Chicagoland. It won eleven Emmys in 2024, then a record for a comedy in one year, even though many viewers think of it as a drama.
hook: 'Yes, chef': a comedy that plays like a panic attack.

question: Which 2025 Ryan Coogler film set a record with 16 Academy Award nominations?
explanation: It passed the 14 nominations shared by All About Eve, Titanic and La La Land. Michael B. Jordan won Best Actor for playing twin brothers Smoke and Stack, but Best Picture went to One Battle After Another.
hook: One actor, two twins, sixteen nominations.

question: Which 2025 Netflix drama about a 13-year-old boy accused of murder shot every episode in one continuous take?
explanation: Co-created by Stephen Graham and Jack Thorne, it set off a national debate in Britain about online misogyny. Owen Cooper, in his first screen role, became the youngest male Emmy winner at fifteen.
hook: Four episodes, four single takes, and a first-time actor who won an Emmy.

question: Which 1990s Australian school drama did Netflix reboot in 2022?
explanation: The original ran from 1994 to 1999, first on Ten and then the ABC. The reboot is set at the same Hartley High, and autistic actor Chloé Hayden plays the autistic character Quinni.
hook: Same Hartley High, twenty-eight years later.

question: Which Sydney-raised rapper topped the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2021 with 'Stay', a duet with Justin Bieber?
explanation: Born Charlton Howard, he grew up in Redfern and Waterloo and has Kamilaroi heritage. 'Stay' spent seven weeks at number one in the US.
hook: LAROI comes from Kamilaroi, his mob.

question: Which song holds the record for most weeks at number one on the Australian ARIA singles chart, with 24?
distractors: Somebody That I Used to Know
explanation: Toni Watson, who performs as Tones and I, wrote it about crowds when she was busking in Byron Bay. It passed the Australian record held by Bing Crosby's 'White Christmas', which had lasted since the 1940s.
hook: A Byron Bay busker beat Bing Crosby.

question: Which Australian actress won an Emmy for playing Shiv Roy in the final season of Succession?
explanation: Adelaide-born Snook won Lead Actress in a Drama at the Emmys held in January 2024, the first Australian to win that category. Elizabeth Debicki, the tempting wrong answer, played Princess Diana in The Crown.
hook: Snook played the Roy daughter; Debicki played the princess.

question: Which HBO Max hospital series won the Emmy for Outstanding Drama in both 2025 and 2026?
explanation: Noah Wyle, who played Dr Carter in ER, stars as the head of a Pittsburgh emergency department, and won Best Actor in 2025. Each season covers one fifteen-hour shift, with each episode showing one hour of it.
hook: One shift per season, one hour per episode.
